2025-26 Carolina Hurricanes

The Carolina Hurricanes surged through the first three rounds with the best record by a team entering a Stanley Cup Final under the best-of-seven format (since 1987) and stormed back in a championship series for the ages to win the Stanley Cup for the second time in franchise history – five days shy of the 20-year anniversary of the franchise’s first title.

 

Carolina occupied a playoff spot the entire season; sat in first place in the Metropolitan Division from Dec. 11 onward; clinched an eighth consecutive postseason berth; and lost only one game against the Ottawa Senators (4‑0 in R1), Philadelphia Flyers (4‑0 in R2) and Montreal Canadiens (4‑1 in CF) to reach the championship series, where it reeled off three straight wins to overcome a 2‑1 deficit and defeat the Vegas Golden Knights in a historic Stanley Cup Final:

 

* In Game 1 (5‑4 VGK W), Vegas became the first road team in NHL history to open a Stanley Cup Final with a multi-goal comeback victory.

 

* In Game 2 (4‑3 CAR OT W), Carolina became the first team in 82 years to win a Stanley Cup Final game when trailing by multiple goals in the final 10 minutes of regulation.

 

* In Game 3 (5‑4 VGK 2OT W), Golden Knights right wing Mitch Marner registered the fastest hat trick in Stanley Cup Final history (and became the second player with a four-point period in the championship round) before the Hurricanes scored the fastest three goals by one team in a Stanley Cup Final en route to recording the second instance of a team erasing a deficit of four or more goals in a Stanley Cup Final game.

 

* In Game 4 (5‑3 CAR W), Vegas rallied from a 3‑1 hole to make the series the first Stanley Cup Final to feature a team erasing a multi-goal deficit to at least tie the score in each of the first four contests.

 

* In Game 5 (4‑2 CAR W), Hurricanes captain Jordan Staal became the fourth player in NHL history – and first in 70 years – to score a goal in each of the first five games of a Stanley Cup Final.

 

* In Game 6 (3‑0 CAR W), Carolina’s Brandon Bussi became the third goaltender – and first in 89 years – to earn a Stanley Cup-clinching shutout during his first NHL season.

 

The Hurricanes went 16‑3 during the entirety of the postseason, trailing only the 1988 Edmonton Oilers (16‑2) for the fewest losses by a Stanley Cup champion since all four rounds went to the best-of-seven format in 1987.

 

Rod Brind’Amour, who first hoisted the trophy with Carolina in 2006, became the fourth individual in NHL history to captain a Stanley Cup winner and then lead that team to another championship as its head coach. He joined Toe Blake (w/ MTL), Hap Day (w/ TOR) and Cooney Weiland (w/ BOS).

2024-25 Florida Panthers
The Florida Panthers repeated as champions by defeating the same opponent – the Edmonton Oilers – in the 11th Stanley Cup Final rematch in NHL history and first since 2008 and 2009 (DET vs. PIT).

The Panthers lost in overtime in the opening game of the series, but won four of the next five contests (outscoring the Oilers 25-13 over that span) to become the 10th franchise in League history to repeat as champions and third to do so in the 21st century, joining the Pittsburgh Penguins (2016 and 2017) and Tampa Bay Lightning (2020 and 2021).

Florida scored 94 goals during the 2025 Stanley Cup Playoffs (23 GP) – the highest single-year number by one team since the 1991 Penguins (95 in 24 GP) – including 28 during their six-game triumph over Edmonton, tied for the second-highest total by any team in a Stanley Cup Final.

The Panthers’ run to their repeat included a 10-3 postseason record as visitors, matching the most road wins by one team in a single playoff year. Their 61 road goals established a League record, ahead of the 49 scored by the 1993 Los Angeles Kings (13 GP).

Aleksander Barkov (Tampere, Finland) became the first European player captain multiple Stanley Cup champions.

2023-24 Florida Panthers

The Florida Panthers capped their 30th NHL season by winning their first Stanley Cup, one year and 11 days after falling in the Final to the Vegas Golden Knights.

 

The Panthers became the ninth team in NHL history to win the Stanley Cup after losing in the previous Final, and first since the 2009 Pittsburgh Penguins (also 1984 EDM, 1968 MTL, 1956 MTL, 1953 MTL, 1950 DET, 1943 DET and 1933 NYR).

 

Florida, which raced to a 3‑0 series lead in the Stanley Cup Final, secured its first championship with a 2‑1 victory over the Edmonton Oilers in Game 7. The Panthers became the second team in NHL history to earn a Game 7 win in the Final despite surrendering a 3‑0 series lead, following the 1945 Toronto Maple Leafs.

 

Aleksander Barkov (Tampere, Finland) became the first Finnish-born player in League history to captain a Stanley Cup-winning team and the fifth NHL player born and trained outside North America to do so, joining Gabriel Landeskog (2022 COL), Alex Ovechkin (2018 WSH), Zdeno Chara (2011 BOS) and Nicklas Lidstrom (2008 DET). He also led Florida and ranked fifth in the playoffs with 8‑14—22 (24 GP).

 

At 35 years, 278 days, Sergei Bobrovsky became the 11th goaltender in NHL history to secure a Stanley Cup-clinching win at age 35 or older and just the fifth to do so in the past 55 years, following Tim Thomas (2011 BOS), Chris Osgood (2008 DET), Dominik Hasek (2002 DET) and Patrick Roy (2001 COL).

2022-23 Vegas Golden Knights

Eight days shy of the seven-year anniversary of Las Vegas officially receiving an NHL franchise and 2,076 days after the team’s first regular-season game, the Vegas Golden Knights became Stanley Cup champions.

 

The Golden Knights clinched their first title with a 9-3 victory over the Florida Panthers in Game 5 of the Stanley Cup Final, the southernmost championship series in League history.

 

Vegas, playing its sixth season, became the second-fastest franchise in the NHL’s modern era (since 1943‑44) to win the Stanley Cup, a mark only bested by the Edmonton Oilers (5th season in 1983‑84).

 

Six players who played for the Golden Knights during their inaugural campaign were on the Stanley Cup-winning squad: William Carrier, William Karlsson, Jonathan Marchessault, Brayden McNabb, Reilly Smith and Shea Theodore. All six also skated with the team in its five-game loss to the Washington Capitals in the 2018 Stanley Cup Final.

 

Vegas became the second team in as many years to not face elimination en route to winning the Stanley Cup (also 2022 COL). In fact, the Golden Knights only trailed in a series once, dropping their playoff opener vs. WPG before going 16‑5 the rest of the postseason.

2021-22 Colorado Avalanche

The Colorado Avalanche dethroned the two-time defending champion Tampa Bay Lightning in six games in the Final to win the Stanley Cup for the third time in franchise history (also 1995‑96 and 2000‑01).

 

Colorado claimed its championship by going 16‑4 in the playoffs, becoming the sixth team since 1987 (when all four rounds went to the best-of-seven format) to capture the Stanley Cup with four or fewer postseason losses.

 

Overall, the Avalanche – who set franchise records for wins (56) and points (119) during the regular season – posted 72 combined victories in 2021‑22, tied for the most in a single season in NHL history (w/ 1976‑77 MTL, 1983‑84 EDM and 1995‑96 DET).

 

Colorado concluded the postseason with a 9‑1 record as visitors, one shy of the League benchmark for road wins in a playoff year, and became the fourth Stanley Cup champions in NHL history to earn each of its four series-clinching victories on the road (also 2007‑08 DET, 2008‑09 PIT and 2017‑18 WSH).

 

Ten of the Avalanche’s playoff wins (including all four series-clinchers) were achieved in comeback fashion, tied with the 2008‑09 Pittsburgh Penguins for the most in a single postseason.

2020-21 Tampa Bay Lightning

After the Tampa Bay Lightning won the 2019-20 Stanley Cup during an elongated season that took 363 days due to a pause caused by the COVID‑19 pandemic, they again hoisted the prized trophy just 282 days later.

 

Tampa Bay claimed its third championship in franchise history, adding to titles won in 2003-04 and 2019-20, with a 1-0 victory over the Montreal Canadiens in Game 5 of the Final. The Lightning became the ninth different franchise to repeat as Stanley Cup champions and the fifth to do so among teams that joined the NHL in 1967‑68 or later, following the Edmonton Oilers, New York Islanders, Philadelphia Flyers and Pittsburgh Penguins.

 

The Lightning’s championship journey included the first-ever all-Florida matchup in the Stanley Cup Playoffs, a six-game victory over the Florida Panthers in the First Round, followed by a five-game triumph against the Discover NHL Central Division’s top-seeded Carolina Hurricanes in the Second Round. In an epic final-four rematch with the Islanders, the Lightning emerged from the Stanley Cup Semifinals with their sixth all-time Game 7 victory, setting up a meeting with the Canadiens in the Final.

2019-20 Tampa Bay Lightning

Nearly a full year after the opening face-off of the 2019-20 campaign and more than six months after the League hit “pause” on the regular season due to the COVID‑19 pandemic, the Tampa Bay Lightning won Game 6 of the Final versus the Dallas Stars to claim their second Stanley Cup.

 

The clinching victory came 363 days after the puck dropped on the regular season, 201 days after the pause began and 65 days after players entered “bubbles” in Edmonton and Toronto for a postseason unlike any other in League history.

 

The Lightning became the first franchise to join the NHL in the 1990s or later and win the Stanley Cup multiple times, though the trophy presentation looked quite different than the first time in 2004.

 

Former captain Dave Andreychuk accepted the team’s first Stanley Cup on June 7, 2004, after Game 7 against the Calgary Flames in front of a crowd of 22,717 fans at St. Pete Times Forum, while Steven Stamkos received the trophy on Sept. 28, 2020, alongside the entire team inside an empty Rogers Place in Edmonton.

2018-19 St. Louis Blues

The St. Louis Blues defeated the Boston Bruins in Game 7 of the Final to win their first Stanley Cup in the franchise’s 52-year history, capping an unprecedented season in which they became the first team in the NHL’s expansion era (since 1967‑68) to win a championship after ranking last in the overall League standings at any point after their 30th game.

 

The Blues ended the longest wait in NHL history – 51 seasons – for a team to win its first championship; St. Louis eclipsed the Los Angeles Kings, who held the distinction after winning the Stanley Cup for the first time in 2011‑12, their 44th season.

 

The Blues (No. 12 in NHL) became the second team to win the Stanley Cup after finishing the regular season ranked 12th or lower in the overall League standings, also following the 2012 Kings (No. 13 in NHL).

 

St. Louis became the fourth team in the modern era (since 1943‑44) – and first in 30 years – to win the Stanley Cup without a previous winner on its roster, joining the 1974 Philadelphia Flyers, 1980 New York Islanders and 1989 Calgary Flames.

2017-18 Washington Capitals

The Washington Capitals won their first Stanley Cup in their 43rd NHL season, spoiling the Vegas Golden Knights’ unprecedented run for a championship in their inaugural campaign.

 

Washington ended the second-longest wait for an NHL team before winning its first Stanley Cup; the Los Angeles Kings captured the 2012 title in their 44th campaign. The Capitals’ win also ended a championship drought for fans of metro D.C. pro sports teams, who hadn’t celebrated a championship since Washington’s NFL team won the Super Bowl in 1992.

 

Washington’s come-from-behind, Stanley Cup-clinching win in Game 5 capped a thrilling roller-coaster playoff ride for the team and its fans.

 

Over the course of two months, the Capitals overcame a pair of home overtime losses to start the postseason in the First Round against the Columbus Blue Jackets; vanquished the Pittsburgh Penguins, who eliminated them in each of their prior seven playoff series and in nine of 10 series overall; rallied from a three-game losing streak to defeat the Tampa Bay Lightning in the Eastern Conference Final, including a road win in Game 7; and topped former Penguins goaltender Marc-Andre Fleury and the Golden Knights in the Final.

2016-17 Pittsburgh Penguins

The Pittsburgh Penguins won their fifth Stanley Cup – and second straight – with a six-game victory over the Nashville Predators in the Final.

 

The Penguins became the first team to repeat as champions since the Detroit Red Wings in 1997 and 1998, accomplishing the feat for the second time in franchise history (also 1991 and 1992).

 

Patric Hornqvist, who was selected by the Predators with the final pick (230th overall) of the 2005 NHL Draft and played his first six seasons in Nashville, scored with 1:35 remaining in regulation to break a scoreless tie in Game 6 of the Final and lift the Penguins to their championship.

 

Hornqvist became the third player to score a Stanley Cup-clinching goal in the final two minutes of regulation (all on the road). The others: Bill Carson in 1929 (18:02 w/ BOS) and Dave Bolland in 2013 (19:01 w/ CHI).

The Pittsburgh Penguins skated their way to a fourth Stanley Cup, capturing the title exactly seven years to the day after their most recent triumph in 2009.

 

Defenseman Kris Letang scored the Stanley Cup-winning goal against the San Jose Sharks in Game 6 of the Final and factored on all four of Pittsburgh’s game-winning goals during the series.

2014-15 Chicago Blackhawks

The Chicago Blackhawks captured their sixth Stanley Cup in franchise history – and third in six seasons – by clinching the title on home ice for the first time since April 12, 1938.

 

They became the first team to win three Stanley Cups in a six-year span since the Detroit Red Wings did so from 1997 through 2002.
